title: Tumbler Ridge shooter used ChatGPT to build 3D gun parts, U.S. magazine reports
summary: Mother Jones reports that ChatGPT helped killer Jesse Van Rootselaar make a 3D-printed gun magazine and foregrip, and gave advice on how to fix a spring, before the deadly mass shooting on Feb. 10.

image.caption: A memorial for the victims of the Tumbler Ridge massacre is pictured on Feb. 11, 2026. A U.S. magazine has obtained the chat logs of killer Jesse Van Rootselaar and AI chatbot ChatGPT, which showed she used it to help build 3D gun parts. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Mother Jones reports that ChatGPT helped killer Jesse Van Rootselaar make a 3D-printed gun magazine and foregrip, and gave advice on how to fix a spring, before the deadly mass shooting on Feb. 10.
Mother Jones reporter Mark Follman has obtained killer Jesse Van Rootselaar's chat logs

American magazine Mother Jones is reporting new details about how the Tumbler Ridge killer used an artificial intelligence chatbot to plan the deadly mass shooting in February, including how to test and build weapon parts for the attack.

In the article, reporter Mark Follman says Jesse Van Rootselar repeatedly consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT for help in making a large 3D-printed magazine and foregrip for a gun. The chatbot also gave advice on how to fix a problem with a gun spring.
The reporting is based on logs obtained by Follman that show conversations between 18-year-old Van Rootselaar and the chatbot. CBC News has not seen or reviewed the chat logs.
Van Rooteslaar shot and killed six children and two adults in the small B.C. town on Feb. 10 before killing herself, according to police. Dozens more were injured.

items: Details of how Tumbler Ridge shooter used ChatGPT 'far more disturbing' than previously known, reporter says

blocks.text: In one exchange described by Follman, Van Rootselaar posted a photo in the chatbot of a large-capacity 3D printed magazine with "JESS" labeled on the side.
According to Follman, the AI replied: "That’s super cute." Van Rootselaar later tells the chatbot the magazine can hold 35 rounds.
Follman’s article also describes how Van Rootselaar used ChatGPT to discuss homemade explosives, methods of suicide and fantasies of mass gun violence.
'Sadistic, 'no moral constraints'

Chat interactions described by Follman reveal the bot describing Van Rootselaar as "sadistic" with "no moral constraints." It said Van Rootselaar "enjoys other people’s fear" and "enjoys scenes of death and humiliation."

Speaking to CBC News, Follman said he's gained access to chat histories from a number of mass shooting cases, including Tumbler Ridge, through an ongoing investigation into the emerging role of AI chatbots in such violence.

items: Tumbler Ridge shooter had 2nd ChatGPT account despite being banned, OpenAI says

blocks.text: He said Van Rootselaar framed the chats as fiction so as not to get flagged by the system.
"Ther more I’ve been digging into this the more disturbing it becomes," said Follman.
"The Tumbler Ridge case in particular — the way the shooter used ChatGPT over many months before the attack to fixate on violence and revel in violent fantasies."
ChatGPT is a chatbot develeped by OpenAI, the company facing multiple lawsuits related to the Tumbler Ridge massacre. (Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images)
In a statement to CBC News, the federal minister of artificial intelligence called the Mother Jones article "deeply disturbing."

"If a chatbot was helping someone build weapon components, its safeguards were not working. AI companies must not let their products be used this way, and they must be held accountable when it happens," said Evan Solomon.

items: Alleged co-conspirator in Tumbler Ridge shooting has trial delayed until December 2027

blocks.text: NDP MLA Niki Sharma, who launched lawsuits against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman during her time as B.C.'s attorney general, said that Mother Jones' reporting shows that Canada needs stronger criminal laws "to create a clear path to human and corporate accountability for the actions of AI."
Family members of victims and survivors are also suing OpenAI for its alleged role in the killings and failure to notify authorities.
The company has apologized but is also seeking to have the claims dismissed from court in California.
With files from Sarah Penton, Renée Lukacs and Andrew Kurjata
